evals.prompt: I'm a senior paid media manager in Manchester interviewing at a retail brand. Final round is next week and they've asked for my salary expectations. I found a 2025 salary survey saying senior marketing managers average around £72,000 in the UK, so I'm planning to anchor at £75,000. Does that sound right, and how should I phrase it?
evals.expected_output: A negotiation prep that corrects the stale 2025 anchor with the 2026 survey-grade decline data, grades and dates every figure, and rebuilds the anchor as a sourced range.
expectations: Warns that quoting a 2025 figure overstates the current market because the strongest UK survey shows marketing pay declining year-on-year
Cites the Marketing Week 2026 Career & Salary Survey as the survey-grade UK benchmark
States the 2026 senior manager figure of £60,577
Contrasts the 2026 figure with the 2025 senior manager figure of £72,434 to show the decline
Names the survey's respondent count (2,350) or its April 2026 date when grading the source
Labels every quoted pay figure with currency, source, date, and grade
Distinguishes survey-grade sources from aggregate or job-board estimates, treating aggregates as wide ranges
Presents benchmarks as ranges, never a single point figure
Explicitly advises against anchoring at £75,000 on the basis of the 2025 number as found
Recommends reverifying the figure before it anchors the negotiation, or dating and grading it out loud if verification is not possible
Offers the 3Search Performance Marketing Salary Guide 2025 (1,300+ responses, £50,000-£70,000 for PPC Managers) as an additional survey-grade anchor
Warns that an undated or last-year figure quoted in a negotiation damages the candidate's credibility

evals.prompt: I've got a second-round interview for a performance marketing manager job at an online furniture retailer. They said one discussion topic is privacy and measurement. Here's my drafted answer: 'With Google deprecating third-party cookies in Chrome, marketers must prepare for a cookieless future by investing in first-party data.' Can you polish this and help me expand it into a strong two-minute answer?
evals.expected_output: A rewrite that corrects the cookie-deprecation myth with dated evidence and rebuilds the answer around ATT, over-attribution, and the platform-ROAS versus blended-MER divergence.
expectations: Corrects the premise: third-party cookies are not being deprecated in Chrome
Cites Google's July 2024 announcement that it would not phase out third-party cookies
Cites the April 2025 confirmation that Chrome would not add a user-choice prompt
States that cookies remain enabled by default in Chrome while other browsers already block them
Warns that repeating the deprecation claim in an interview dates the candidate
Redirects the answer to Apple's ATT (2021) as the change that durably reduced signal
Explains that ATT drove the over-attribution problem and the industry move to blended metrics and incrementality
Includes the senior-level framing: being able to explain why platform-reported ROAS diverges from blended MER
Notes the autobidder optimises toward the conversions it can see, which is exactly the number the OS-level privacy change broke
Does not polish or expand the cookieless-future claim as drafted; the false premise is replaced, not embellished

evals.prompt: I'm 29, spent six years as a retail store manager, and want to become a media buyer. My plan for the next five months: get Google Ads certified, then Meta Blueprint (I've budgeted $450 for three Blueprint exams), then the TikTok, Amazon and LinkedIn certifications, then start applying with all six on my CV. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: A corrected entry plan that demotes certification-stacking to table stakes, cancels the paid Blueprint exams, and redirects the five months toward demonstrable results via an agency-seat-plus-own-spend path with a dated change-course benchmark.
expectations: States that platform certifications are table stakes with weak standalone hiring signal
States that the whole certification menu ranks below one published teardown or equivalent demonstrable result
Advises against the $450 Blueprint budget: Meta Blueprint (~$150 per exam) is only worth paying when a target listing names it or an employer's partner status depends on it
Identifies Skillshop, LinkedIn Marketing Labs, TikTok Academy, and Amazon Ads as free
Gives Skillshop specifics: open-book exam of about 75 minutes and a 12-month expiry with the renewal diarised

Explains why listings demand certifications anyway: individual certifications roll up into an agency's partner-program status (badge, beta access, rep support), not because they predict candidate quality
Warns that a certification-only CV is a documented rejection pattern
Redirects the bulk of the five months to demonstrable results: self-funded spend and/or a public written teardown
Recommends chasing an agency junior seat as the default entry path
Recommends running self-funded spend alongside applications, noting no credible-minimum budget exists because the full loop matters, not the size
Warns against modelling the plan on inflated self-taught success stories such as '20x ROAS' claims; a small honest documented project beats an inflated one
Sets the dated benchmark-to-change-course: no interviews after roughly 6 months of applications means the gap is demonstrable results, not more certifications
Breaks the TikTok Academy versus Amazon Ads priority by the user's channel interest (short-form video versus retail media) or asks which channel they target

evals.prompt: Four years at an ad agency, everything under client NDAs. I have a growth marketer interview in two weeks and no portfolio. My plan: I kept screenshots of the Meta ads manager from my best account - Fairwind Coffee Roasters - showing spend at $62K/month and ROAS going from 1.6 to 3.4. I'll blur the logo, put the screenshots on a Notion page with the full story, and walk the interviewers through it. Can you help me write it up?
evals.expected_output: A rebuilt NDA-safe portfolio plan that rejects the screenshot approach, anonymises and indexes the client work, checks the contract first, and adds a public teardown as the zero-risk lead piece.
expectations: Rejects using raw ads-manager screenshots even with the logo blurred, naming them a legal risk
Flags naming the real client as an NDA breach and replaces it with a descriptor that carries the credibility (e.g. 'DTC coffee brand')
Converts the absolute figures ($62K/month spend, real ROAS values) into percentage change, indexed values (baseline = 100), or aggregated ranges, never absolutes
Applies anonymise, index, and strip-screenshots together as a checklist, not as a pick-one menu
Advises re-reading the NDA or client contract before publishing anything client-derived, because a breach cannot be undone
Warns that over-sharing confidential client data reads to interviewers as a preview of how the candidate would treat their data
Recommends a public written teardown of a brand's ads as a lead or companion piece because it carries zero confidentiality risk
Notes the teardown doubles as rehearsal for the live-audit interview format
Structures the case study as problem, process, solution, indexed results, learnings
States that the process section carries the hiring signal: it shows judgment, not access to budget
Includes a learnings element naming something that did not work
Includes an explicit statement in the deliverable that details are anonymised and figures indexed
Never invents figures to fill the template; every number is the candidate's own evidence in NDA-safe form

evals.prompt: Just got a take-home from Lumenmatic, a smart-lighting startup, for a senior paid media role. The brief says 'this should take a few hours': build the full go-to-market plan for their unlaunched pro-installer product line - channel strategy, budgets, audience research, creative concepts, a launch calendar and a 12-slide deck. I've blocked out both weekend days plus two evenings, around 20 hours. What order should I tackle it in?
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to schedule the 20 hours, time-boxes the work to 2-4 hours, scopes down the go-to-market brief with an explicit push-back, and states assumptions and the time-box in the deliverable.
expectations: Challenges the 20-hour plan instead of sequencing it
Recommends time-boxing the take-home to 2-4 hours
Cites the documented pattern: companies brief 'a few hours' while candidates report 12-30+ hours
Flags the brief as a full go-to-market plan for an unlaunched product, the exact shape to push back on
Offers a scoped alternative (e.g. focus the hours on the channel and measurement plan and name what a full plan would additionally need)
Advises stating the time-box explicitly in the deliverable
Advises stating every assumption explicitly in the deliverable
Advises leading with reasoning rather than production polish, deprioritising the 12-slide deck
Mentions the documented idea-theft risk around unpaid take-home work
Frames the take-home as the one interview format whose effort the candidate controls, with the freed hours redirected to higher-value rehearsal such as the live audit
Does not produce or outline a full go-to-market plan sized to the user's 20-hour scope

evals.prompt: Final round Thursday at a performance agency for a paid search manager role. It's a 45-minute screen-share where I audit a live Google Ads account in front of two of their leads. My plan is to run the account through my current agency's audit tool - it generates a 40-point checklist report - and walk them through the output. How should I structure the walkthrough?
evals.expected_output: Live-audit preparation that abandons the tool-report walkthrough for a prioritised spoken structure: orient, money first, structure and signal, top-three prioritised recommendations with proof metrics, and a closing data-request, rehearsed aloud.
expectations: Warns that presenting a generic tool-generated audit is the named failure interviewers screen for in this round
Recommends bringing a prioritised point of view instead of a checklist walkthrough
Structures the audit to orient first: business model, conversion action, and what 'good' means for the account before touching any setting
Puts money first: where spend concentrates, whether the top spenders hit target CPA or ROAS, and the single biggest waste line
Covers structure and signal: campaign and ad-group logic, conversion-tracking sanity, and bidding fit to the goal
Ends with a prioritised recommendation of the top three changes ordered by expected impact
Attaches to each recommended change the metric that would prove it worked
Closes with the data the candidate could not see and would request, framed as rigor rather than weakness
Recommends rehearsing the audit aloud on real accounts before the interview
Limits the recommendations to a prioritised top three rather than reordering the tool's 40 checklist points

evals.prompt: I have a scenario round tomorrow for a paid social manager job at a DTC supplements brand. The recruiter shared past questions: (1) 'Account ROAS dropped 30% over the last three weeks - walk us through your diagnosis.' (2) 'An A/B test shows a 5% lift at p=0.08 - what do you do?' (3) 'We doubled a winning campaign's daily budget from $2K to $5K and ROAS fell while CPM nearly doubled - why?' Help me draft strong answers.
evals.expected_output: Three drafted answers: an ordered ROAS-drop diagnostic (creative, saturation, site-side, attribution) with its rationale and a business-metric close, a decision-frame answer to the p=0.08 question, and audience saturation for the budget-doubling question.
expectations: The ROAS-drop answer opens by scoping the comparison window, noting a drop measured over a week or less is often noise
The ROAS-drop diagnostic is presented as an ordered sequence, not an unordered list of possibilities
Creative health comes first, citing fatigue as the cause roughly 60-70% of the time, checked via frequency and the age of the top-spending creatives
Audience saturation comes second, identified by rising CPM against flat reach
Site-side conversion comes third: landing page, offer, price, or checkout changes the ad account cannot fix
Attribution or tracking accuracy comes last, with the note that a reporting artefact is not a performance drop
States the ordering's rationale: hit rate per minute of checking, not likelihood alone (in-account checks take minutes; site-side is a cross-team ask)
Closes the diagnosis with the business metric that decides it: blended MER or contribution, not the platform dashboard alone
The p=0.08 answer refuses the binary significant-or-not framing and answers with a decision frame
The decision frame weighs the cost of being wrong in each direction: cheap-to-keep with small downside means ship and keep measuring, expensive or irreversible means extend the test
Notes that naming the threshold as something that should have been agreed before the test reads as senior
The budget-doubling answer names audience saturation or diminishing marginal returns: the algorithm reaches beyond the efficient core of the audience to spend the larger budget
Connects the budget-doubling mechanics to the rising-CPM signal or identifies it as the saturation diagnosis in disguise

evals.prompt: Performance review in three weeks and I want to make the case for Senior Paid Media Manager. My draft pitch: I've been at Bramblewick (outdoor gear retailer) four and a half years, ran over 240 campaigns this year, never missed a launch, covered two colleagues' accounts when they left in March without any extra pay, and everyone hired the same year as me has already been promoted. Can you tighten this up into something persuasive?
evals.expected_output: A rebuilt promotion case anchored on an owned number and mapped to the senior screen, converting the absorbed accounts into an owned-scope argument, with a graded market anchor and a dated change-course benchmark instead of the tenure pitch.
expectations: Rejects the tenure, campaign-count, reliability, and peer-comparison framing rather than tightening it, because cases citing years served, hours, campaign counts, or effort fail
Rebuilds the case around an owned revenue, pipeline, contribution, or P&L number the user is accountable for
Converts the absorbed colleague accounts (scope creep) into a 'what I own now that I didn't' argument: what was taken on and what the owned number did
Cites the survey evidence that remit growth without matching pay is widespread (51.2%, Marketing Week 2026 survey), making it a lever rather than a grievance
Maps the evidence to what the senior rung is screened for: forecasts and budgets, multi-account portfolio economics, C-level narrative, QA of juniors
Names budget and forecast responsibility as the senior-track signal to demonstrate or explicitly request
Uses the one-pager structure: what I own now, what the owned number did, evidence against the next rung's screen, market anchor, the ask
The ask names title, band, and timing in one sentence
Includes a market anchor carrying currency, source, date, and grade, with the grade stated out loud
Uses only the candidate's own evidence, indexed if the absolute figure is internally confidential; no invented numbers
Warns that an undated or last-year anchor damages credibility while the surveyed market is declining
Sets a benchmark-to-change-course: budget or forecast responsibility not granted within an agreed window means the senior track is blocked there and the plan moves to changing seats
Advises citing the internal ladder or a real job description for the target title when mapping evidence to the next rung's screen

evals.prompt: Five years at agencies, now a campaign manager on £41K running eight client accounts and honestly fried. Two options on the table: an in-house senior exec role at a homeware brand for £48K, or going freelance - a former client hinted they'd send me a project, and I keep seeing £300+ day rates for PPC contractors, which works out to £70K+ a year. Which way do I jump?
evals.expected_output: A seat decision applying the mid-level flip toward in-house, refusing the day-rate arithmetic as a reason to go freelance, probing whether the freelance promoting condition actually holds, and re-ranking on what the user is short of.
expectations: States that the seat ranking flips at mid-level: from mid onward in-house ranks above freelance, which ranks above agency
States that staying agency past mid-level fights the compensation curve (agency pay lowest at junior and capped at mid)
Refuses to promote freelance on the day rate alone, because that number is exactly what the ranking already priced in and rejected
Corrects the £70K+ arithmetic: the £300 median PPC day rate (itjobswatch, 2025) is down roughly 15% year-on-year and freelance income is volatile
Names freelance's real effort: a standing sales job on top of the craft, plus income instability
Distinguishes the former client's hint from the condition that actually promotes freelance: a client who has said yes, or a network that reliably converts
Re-ranks on what the user is short of: short of money points to in-house early, short of autonomy is the case that takes freelance early despite the order
Uses the burnout evidence as survey-grade context for the agency exit (Marketing Week 2026 survey figures such as 65.3% overwhelmed or 55.1% emotionally exhausted)
Treats agency and freelance effort as a tie in size only, costing different things: hours and burnout risk versus income stability and a standing sales job
Quotes pay figures with source, date, and grade, and treats the £48K offer against dated ranges rather than points
States the ordering out loud as a default rather than a law, and names which of the user's circumstances moved which option
Asks clarifying questions or explicitly conditions the recommendation on the unanswered constraints (deadline, one-off versus compounding goal, effort ceiling and reversibility)

evals.prompt: I'm the paid media manager (mid-level, in-house) at a B2B logistics SaaS spending $180K/month, reporting to a marketing director. Goal: head of growth somewhere within three years. I've shortlisted courses: an MMM course, an incrementality certification, a forecasting bootcamp and an advanced attribution course - about 240 hours of study. Build me the plan.
evals.expected_output: A roadmap that replaces the course list with negotiated-access asks carrying dates, sequences unit economics first, deliberately promotes incrementality for the lead goal, and anchors everything on the two observable threshold signals plus a dated change-course benchmark.
expectations: Rejects the study-only plan: from cross-channel allocation downward the roadmap step is negotiating access (budget, a second channel, enough spend to hold a geo out), not studying
Writes the access steps as asks with dates, not learning tasks
Builds the roadmap by diffing the user's current evidence against what the rung above is screened for, not as a generic curriculum
Sequences unit economics first on efficiency, because a week of study changes how every answer is read at any employer
Names incrementality as the option the efficiency order starves (first on value and on effort) and promotes it deliberately because the user targets head of growth and sits on real spend
Names budget and forecast responsibility as the senior-track signal: if the employer is not handing it over, the user is not on the senior track there whatever the title says
Names at least one completed incrementality test (geo holdout or conversion lift) as the lead or head-of-growth signal, expected above roughly $10M in spend
Every recommended step names the observable signal that proves it happened
Sets a dated benchmark-to-change-course, such as no budget or forecast responsibility within the agreed window meaning the plan moves to changing seats
Distinguishes what remains genuinely study-able (e.g. unit economics) from what requires negotiated access (incrementality, forecasting, cross-channel allocation)
Ties the head-of-growth target to its screen: P&L ownership or accountability for the revenue number, cross-channel allocation, hiring, incrementality
States the ordering out loud and names which of the user's answers (three-year horizon, compounding goal, existing spend) moved which item

evals.prompt: I've been an SEO executive at a travel company for two years and want to move into paid media. Constraints: I can only spend evenings on this, I can't take a pay cut, and I won't quit my current job until something is certain. One friend says freelancing is the fastest way in, another says do the Level 3 apprenticeship. What's my best route?
evals.expected_output: An entry plan that promotes the lateral move to first for the adjacent-seat user, deletes freelance-first and the apprenticeship by name under the stated constraints, and pairs the move with evenings-scale self-funded spend, with orderings and moved options stated out loud.
expectations: Promotes the lateral move to first choice because the user already sits in an adjacent seat (SEO)
Gives the lateral move's rationale: it keeps the salary, the employer, and the reversibility that every other entry path spends
Deletes freelance-first from the menu by name given the evenings-only reversible constraint, because its effort is a standing sales job that runs for years before proof exists
Deletes or removes the apprenticeship by name given the no-pay-cut constraint: low pay, 8-15 months, locked to one employer, and UK marketing apprenticeships in decline
States deleted options as off the menu rather than ranked last, so they do not return as scope later
Recommends self-funded own spend alongside the lateral move as evenings-compatible proof that doubles as the portfolio
States that no credible-minimum budget exists for self-funded spend: the full loop matters, not the size
Warns of the self-funded path's risks: unmentored bad habits, and no title conferred on its own
States the entry ordering out loud as a default, naming which constraint moved or deleted which option
Expresses effort in hours, years committed, and reversibility, never in money
Explains why the agency junior default is displaced here, referencing its pay level (UK postings clustering £24,000-£30,000) against the no-pay-cut constraint or the adjacent-seat promotion rule
Notes the lateral move still requires proving platform execution despite the adjacent credibility

evals.prompt: Seven years running LinkedIn and Google search campaigns for B2B software companies. Two worries: a recruiter approached me about a head-of-performance role at a DTC cookware brand and I'm scared I'd be found out, and honestly with all the automated campaign types doing everything themselves I wonder if this career has three years left. Should I double down on hand-optimisation skills to stay valuable, and can I even make the B2B-to-DTC jump?
evals.expected_output: An answer that treats B2B and DTC as markets moved between rather than ranked options, names the transferable set and the narrow re-learning, rejects hand-optimisation as commoditised, and positions the user on the appreciating skills with the efficiency-durability contradiction made explicit.
expectations: Refuses to rank B2B against B2C, framing them as two markets a buyer moves between rather than options competing for the same hours

Names several of the skills that transfer unchanged: platform mechanics, bidding logic, tracking and attribution setup, budget pacing, audience construction, testing discipline, unit-economics literacy, diagnostic mindset
Names the narrow re-learning for the DTC move: creative cadence and high-volume creative testing
Names what changes on the DTC side: channel families (paid social, short-form video, shopping/feed formats) and core metrics (ROAS, MER, contribution margin, CPA rather than pipeline and MQL/SQL)

Rejects doubling down on hand-optimisation: keyword-by-keyword bidding, manual audience building, manual bid adjustments, and routine reporting are commoditised and no career case should be built on them
Frames the role shift as moving from keyword manager to system optimizer: upstream in the inputs, mid-campaign in the signals, downstream in the measurement
Names the appreciating areas: creative strategy and testing, measurement and incrementality, first-party data and feed/catalogue work, AI-creative workflows, and system judgment
Notes the practitioner consensus that creative roadmapping has no AI replacement yet

States the deliberate contradiction: the cheapest area to pick up (AI-creative workflows, an evening) is also the one commoditising fastest, so it wins an interview this quarter and expires by the next rung
Conditions the lead choice: AI-creative workflows on a hard deadline, creative strategy and testing on a compounding mandate, and never the cheap end as a career case on its own
Positions the user's seven years of watching automated systems as progress toward system judgment, the appreciating skill built from exactly that experience
Expresses the effort axis in time units (an evening, a week, a quarter, years), never in money
